entries.meaning: To present music, a play, or a dance in front of an audience. ---
examples: They perform twice every Saturday.
She performed the whole piece from memory.
The quartet has performed in nineteen countries.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (perform a song), intransitive (perform on stage)

entries.meaning: To play a part in a play, film, or television show. ---
examples: He wants to act, not direct.
She acted in commercials before her first movie.
He has been acting since the age of six.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (act the part of a king), intransitive (act in a film)

entries.meaning: To make music on an instrument, or to perform a piece of music. ---
examples: She plays the cello beautifully.
The band played for three hours without a break.
That song has been played on every station in town.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (play the cello), intransitive (the band played for an hour)
entries.contrast: With an instrument English keeps the: play the piano. With a style it drops the article: play jazz.

entries.meaning: To move your body in time with music. ---
examples: They dance every Friday at the community hall.
She danced the lead in Swan Lake.
He has been dancing since he could walk.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dance a waltz), intransitive (dance all night)
entries.contrast: American /dæns/ with the vowel of cat, not British /dɑːns/.

entries.meaning: To practice a play, concert, or dance before performing it publicly. ---
examples: We rehearse every evening this week.
They rehearsed the fight scene twenty times.
The cast is rehearsing on the real set now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rehearse a scene), intransitive (rehearse all week)

entries.meaning: To try out for a part in a performance, or to hear someone try out. ---
examples: Two hundred singers audition here every year.
She auditioned for the lead and got it.
He is auditioning dancers all afternoon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (audition forty dancers), intransitive (audition for a part)
entries.contrast: A performer auditions for a part; a director auditions the performers.

entries.meaning: To make up music, words, or action as you go, without preparing it. ---
examples: Good actors can improvise when a line is dropped.
The pianist improvised for ten minutes.
They were improvising the entire second half.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (improvise a solo), intransitive (improvise for ten minutes)

entries.meaning: To act something out using only movement, with no words. ---
examples: Street performers mime for the tourists.
He mimed opening a very heavy door.
The singer was obviously miming the words.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (mime opening a door), intransitive (mime on the sidewalk)

entries.meaning: To copy the way someone speaks, moves, or works. ---
examples: Young painters often imitate their teachers.
The parrot imitated the doorbell.
His early songs were clearly imitating Dylan.

entries.meaning: To copy someone's voice or gestures, often to make fun of them. ---
examples: He can mimic any accent in the room.
She mimicked her brother's walk all the way home.
The synthesizer is mimicking a cello.
entries.contrast: A k is inserted before the ending: mimicked, mimicking — like panic → panicked.

entries.meaning: To act out a past event again, in detail. ---
examples: Volunteers reenact the battle every July.
They reenacted the scene for the documentary.
The arrest was reenacted on television.
entries.contrast: Written reenact in American English; the spelling re-enact is also seen.

entries.meaning: To turn a story into a play or film, or to make something sound more exciting than it was. ---
examples: They plan to dramatize the novel for radio.
The papers dramatized a simple disagreement.
Her life has been dramatized twice already.
entries.contrast: American dramatize; British usually dramatise.

entries.meaning: To bend forward from the waist to thank an audience. ---
examples: The cast bows three times on a good night.
She bowed and the applause doubled.
They were still bowing when the curtain came down.
entries.contrast: To bend forward is /baʊ/, rhyming with now. The bow you play a violin with, and the bow in a ribbon, are /boʊ/.

entries.meaning: To bend the knees and lower the body slightly as a formal greeting or thank-you. ---
examples: The ballerinas curtsy at the end of every performance.
She curtsied to the audience and ran off.
The little dancers have been curtsying all evening.
entries.contrast: Consonant + y, so it becomes curtsies and curtsied, but the y stays in curtsying.

entries.meaning: To clap your hands to show that you liked a performance. ---
examples: Some audiences applaud between movements.
They applauded for a full five minutes.
She was applauded before she even sang a note.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (applaud the soloist), intransitive (the crowd applauded)

entries.meaning: To shout in disapproval at a performer or a performance. ---
examples: A few fans always boo the villain.
The crowd booed when the band left after forty minutes.
He has never been booed off a stage.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (boo the villain), intransitive (the crowd booed)
entries.contrast: The double o stays and the ending is simply added: booed, booing.

entries.meaning: To keep several objects moving through the air by throwing and catching them. ---
examples: Clowns juggle while the stage is reset.
He juggled five oranges without dropping one.
She is juggling torches now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (juggle five oranges), intransitive (juggle for the crowd)

entries.meaning: To move your hand or head in order to express something. ---
examples: Actors gesture more broadly on a large stage.
He gestured toward the empty chair.
She was gesturing wildly from the wings.
entries.contrast: You gesture to or gesture toward someone or something.

entries.meaning: To lead people to their seats or through a door. ---
examples: Students usher at the Friday concerts.
An attendant ushered us up to the balcony.
The late guests were ushered in through a side door.

entries.meaning: To signal a performer or a technician to begin. ---
examples: The conductor will cue the horns at bar forty.
He cued the lights a second too early.
The choir is waiting to be cued.
entries.contrast: Both cuing and cueing are correct; American writing prefers cuing.

entries.meaning: To play the leading part in a film or show. ---
examples: She stars in the new comedy.
He starred opposite his own daughter.
The play is starring a complete unknown.
entries.русский: играть главную роль; снимать в главной роли
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the film stars her), intransitive (star in a comedy)
entries.contrast: The r doubles before an ending: starred, starring. An actor stars in a film.

entries.meaning: To be in charge of how a film, play, or piece of music is performed. ---
examples: She directs two shows a season.
He directed the whole film in nineteen days.
The opera is being directed by a newcomer.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (direct a film), intransitive (he writes and directs)

entries.meaning: To put on a play or a public event. ---
examples: The company stages a new musical every fall.
They staged Hamlet in a parking garage.
The whole argument was staged for the cameras.

entries.meaning: To show or perform something publicly for the very first time. ---
examples: The ballet premieres in October.
The film premiered at a small festival in Texas.
Her symphony has already premiered in Chicago.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the theater premiered her play), intransitive (the ballet premieres in October)

entries.meaning: To appear or be presented in public for the first time. ---
examples: Three young singers debut with the orchestra this season.
The show debuted to excellent reviews.
They are debuting two new songs tonight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (debut a new song), intransitive (she debuted at twenty)
entries.contrast: The t is silent: /deɪˈbjuː/, day-BYOO — but it is heard again in debuted, day-BYOOD.

entries.meaning: To be the main act at a concert or festival. ---
examples: Two bands headline on Saturday night.
She headlined the festival at twenty-three.
They are headlining three nights in a row.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (headline the festival), intransitive (two bands headline on Saturday)

entries.meaning: To work together with someone on a creative project. ---
examples: The two composers collaborate constantly.
She collaborated with a choreographer from Havana.
They have collaborated on four albums.
entries.contrast: You collaborate with a person and collaborate on a project.

entries.meaning: To sing or say the same words over and over on one or two notes. ---
examples: The monks chant at dawn.
The crowd chanted her name for five minutes.
The same two lines are chanted throughout the piece.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (chant her name), intransitive (the monks chant at dawn)

entries.meaning: To sing or play notes that fit pleasingly with a melody. ---
examples: The sisters harmonize without even trying.
He harmonized a third below the melody.
They have been harmonizing together since childhood.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (harmonize a melody), intransitive (the sisters harmonize)
entries.contrast: American harmonize; British usually harmonise.

entries.meaning: To lead an orchestra or choir with your hands or a baton. ---
examples: She conducts from the piano.
He conducted the Ninth Symphony from memory.
The concert was conducted by a guest from Vienna.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (conduct the Ninth), intransitive (she conducts from the piano)
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed kuhn-DUKT; the noun conduct, meaning behavior, is KAHN-dukt.

entries.meaning: To arrange music for an orchestra, or to organize something carefully. ---
examples: He orchestrates his own film scores.
She orchestrated the song for forty players.
The whole evening had been carefully orchestrated.

entries.meaning: To play a guitar by sweeping your fingers across the strings. ---
examples: He strums quietly while she sings.
She strummed the same four chords all night.
Someone was strumming on the porch.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (strum a guitar), intransitive (strum quietly)
entries.contrast: The m doubles: strummed, strumming.

entries.meaning: To pull a string with your fingers to make a note. ---
examples: Harpists pluck with both hands.
She plucked the low string once and stopped.
The violins are plucked in this passage.

entries.meaning: To beat a drum, or to tap out a rhythm. ---
examples: He drums for two different bands.
She drummed on the table with a pencil.
Rain was drumming on the roof of the tent.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (drum a rhythm), intransitive (drum for a band)
entries.contrast: The m doubles: drummed, drumming.

entries.meaning: To adjust an instrument so that it plays at the right pitch. ---
examples: Guitarists tune between almost every song.
He tuned the piano the morning of the recital.
The whole orchestra is tuning now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tune a guitar), intransitive (the orchestra is tuning)
entries.contrast: American /tuːn/, TOON; British says /tjuːn/, TYOON.

entries.meaning: To move a piece of music into a different key. ---
examples: Singers often ask you to transpose a song down.
She transposed the aria for a lower voice.
The whole number has been transposed into G.

entries.meaning: To make a new version of a recording by rearranging its parts. ---
examples: Producers remix almost every hit now.
He remixed the single for the clubs.
The track has been remixed four times.
entries.contrast: Ends in -x, so the third person adds -es: remixes.

entries.meaning: To learn something completely, or to prepare the final version of a recording. ---
examples: It takes years to master the violin.
She mastered the piece in under a month.
The album was mastered in Nashville.

entries.meaning: To speak rhyming words in rhythm over a beat. ---
examples: He raps in two languages.
She rapped the last verse alone.
They have been rapping together since high school.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rap a verse), intransitive (rap over a beat)
entries.contrast: The p doubles: rapped, rapping. Sounds exactly like wrapped.

entries.meaning: To sing softly and sweetly, usually a love song. ---
examples: He croons old standards on Sunday nights.
She crooned the baby back to sleep.
A voice was crooning from the radio in the kitchen.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (croon a ballad), intransitive (croon into the microphone)

entries.meaning: To sing or play music for someone, especially outdoors. ---
examples: Strolling musicians serenade the diners.
He serenaded her from the sidewalk below.
We were serenaded through the entire meal.

entries.meaning: To make a loud, harsh sound. ---
examples: The speakers blare until midnight.
A trumpet blared from the balcony.
Music was blaring in the next apartment.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (blare music all night), intransitive (a trumpet blared)

entries.meaning: To make sound and picture, or two performers, match exactly in time. ---
examples: The dancers sync perfectly with the beat.
He synced the audio to the video overnight.
Her lips are not synced with the track.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sync the audio to the video), intransitive (the dancers sync perfectly)
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sink. The longer spelling synch exists, but sync is the usual American form.

entries.meaning: To play or sing alone while the rest of the group stays quiet or accompanies. ---
examples: The saxophone solos after the second chorus.
She soloed for a full three minutes.
He was soloing with his eyes closed.
entries.contrast: The final o stays and -ed is added: soloed, not solod.

entries.meaning: To change something a little from one time to the next, or to be different from one case to another. ---
examples: Try to vary the tempo in the second verse.
She varied the pattern in every panel.
Ticket prices have varied wildly this season.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (vary the tempo), intransitive (prices vary)
entries.contrast: Consonant + y, so it becomes varies and varied, but the y stays in varying.

entries.meaning: To dance a waltz, a smooth dance in three-beat time. ---
examples: The couples waltz slowly around the floor.
They waltzed until the band packed up.
She is waltzing with her grandfather.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (waltz her around the room), intransitive (waltz until midnight)
entries.contrast: Ends in -tz, so the third person adds -es: waltzes.

entries.meaning: To spin around quickly, or to spin something with your fingers. ---
examples: Little girls twirl whenever they get a new dress.
She twirled under his arm and back again.
He was twirling a drumstick between his fingers.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (twirl a baton), intransitive (twirl across the stage)

entries.meaning: To move slowly from side to side. ---
examples: The whole crowd sways during that song.
She swayed in time with the music.
They were swaying with their arms around each other.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the wind swayed the branches), intransitive (sway to the music)

entries.meaning: To put your feet down hard and loudly. ---
examples: The dancers stomp on every downbeat.
He stomped off the stage in the middle of a song.
They were stomping so hard the floor shook.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stomp the floor), intransitive (stomp in time)

entries.meaning: To walk proudly, with your chest out, so that people look at you. ---
examples: Models strut the length of the runway.
He strutted across the stage in a gold jacket.
She was strutting like she owned the place.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (strut the runway), intransitive (strut across the stage)
entries.contrast: The t doubles: strutted, strutting.

entries.meaning: To turn around very fast. ---
examples: The dancers whirl until the music stops.
She whirled around to face the audience.
Skirts were whirling all over the floor.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (whirl a partner around), intransitive (whirl in circles)

entries.meaning: To move easily and happily with the rhythm of music. ---
examples: The whole room grooves when he plays.
We grooved to old soul records all night.
The bass player was grooving with his eyes shut.
entries.русский: двигаться в ритм, ловить кайф от музыки
entries.contrast: You groove to the music.

entries.meaning: To design the steps and movements of a dance. ---
examples: She choreographs for two companies at once.
He choreographed the fight scenes as a dance.
The number was choreographed in a single afternoon.
entries.contrast: The ch is /k/ and the ph is /f/: KOR-ee-uh-graf.

entries.meaning: To walk in a public procession, or to show something off in public. ---
examples: The bands parade down Main Street every June.
The winners paraded through the town.
The costumes were paraded in front of the judges.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (parade the costumes), intransitive (parade down Main Street)

entries.meaning: To darken part of a drawing so that it looks solid or rounded. ---
examples: Shade the left side of the apple so it looks round.
She shaded the background with a soft pencil.
The face still looks flat because you haven't shaded it.

entries.meaning: To give something a light shade of color. ---
examples: One drop of red will tint a whole jar of white paint.
The photographer tinted the old print a warm brown.
The windows have been tinted to cut the glare.

entries.meaning: To draw, paint, or perform something in a particular way. ---
examples: Few painters render light the way he does.
The architect rendered the facade in soft gray.
The aria was beautifully rendered.

entries.meaning: To cut a design into metal or glass with acid or a sharp tool. ---
examples: They etch the design onto a copper plate.
He etched his initials into the glass.
The scene is etched in fine, dark lines.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: etches.

entries.meaning: To paint a shape or letters through a cut-out sheet. ---
examples: They stencil the numbers onto every seat.
She stenciled vines along the top of the wall.
The name was stenciled on the case in white.
entries.contrast: American stenciled, stenciling with one l; British stencilled, stencilling.

entries.meaning: To cut off the edges of a picture or photograph. ---
examples: Crop the photo so the lamp isn't in the corner.
He cropped the image down to a square.
The poster has been badly cropped.
entries.contrast: One vowel plus one consonant, so the p doubles: cropped, cropping.

entries.meaning: To make small changes to a photograph or painting to improve it. ---
examples: Magazines retouch almost every cover.
The lab retouched the scratches out of the negative.
That portrait has clearly been retouched.

entries.meaning: To take a picture of someone or something with a camera. ---
examples: He photographs birds at dawn.
They photographed the whole ceremony.
The painting has never been properly photographed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (photograph a wedding), intransitive (she photographs well)
entries.contrast: The verb keeps the stress on the first syllable, FOH-tuh-graf; photography moves it: fuh-TAH-gruh-fee.

entries.meaning: To make a camera picture larger or smaller without moving the camera. ---
examples: Don't zoom in the middle of a shot.
The camera zoomed slowly onto her face.
He was zooming out to show the whole hall.
entries.contrast: Almost always with in or out: zoom in on a face, zoom out.

entries.meaning: To show work publicly in a gallery or museum. ---
examples: Three local painters exhibit here every spring.
She exhibited in Paris for the first time last year.
His drawings are being exhibited downtown.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (exhibit twenty canvases), intransitive (she exhibits in Paris)
entries.contrast: The h is silent and the x sounds like /ɡz/: ig-ZIB-it.

entries.meaning: To choose and organize the works in a show or a collection. ---
examples: She curates the museum's photography wing.
A student curated the entire exhibit.
The playlist was curated by the band itself.

entries.meaning: To show a new work publicly for the first time. ---
examples: They unveil the statue on Saturday.
The gallery unveiled three new pieces last night.
The mural was unveiled to loud applause.

entries.meaning: To make drawings or models appear to move in a film. ---
examples: They animate every frame by hand.
A small studio animated the opening credits.
The characters were animated in clay.

entries.meaning: To stand for an idea in a work of art. ---
examples: The broken chain symbolizes freedom.
For the poet, winter symbolized old age.
Doves have long symbolized peace.
entries.contrast: American symbolize; British usually symbolise.

entries.meaning: To present something in a way that shows its best qualities. ---
examples: The festival showcases young composers.
The recital showcased her whole range.
Three student films are being showcased tonight.

entries.meaning: To throw an image onto a screen, or to make your voice carry to the back of a hall. ---
examples: Singers learn to project without shouting.
They projected old home movies onto the back wall.
Her voice has always projected well.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (project a film onto the wall), intransitive (learn to project)
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, pruh-JEKT; the noun project is PRAH-jekt.

entries.meaning: To write the words for a film, play, or show. ---
examples: Two writers script every episode.
He scripted the documentary in a single week.
The whole argument was scripted.

entries.meaning: To record something with a movie camera. ---
examples: They film the rehearsals for the archive.
She filmed the whole ceremony on her phone.
The scene was filmed at four in the morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (film a scene), intransitive (they film all summer)

entries.meaning: To speak the lines of a character in an animated film, or to say an opinion aloud. ---
examples: She voices three characters in the same cartoon.
He voiced the villain in both sequels.
The dragon is voiced by a famous actor.

entries.meaning: To broadcast something on television. ---
examples: They televise the awards live every year.
The network televised the final concert.
Opening night was televised around the world.

entries.meaning: To send or watch video or music over the internet as it plays. ---
examples: Thousands stream the show every night.
The band streamed the whole concert for free.
Her new single is streaming everywhere.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stream a concert), intransitive (the song is streaming everywhere)

entries.meaning: To make something widely known to the public. ---
examples: They barely publicize the smaller concerts.
The theater publicized the opening for months.
The tour has been heavily publicized.
entries.contrast: American publicize; British publicise.

entries.meaning: To show great public respect for someone. ---
examples: The festival honors a living composer each year.
They honored him with a lifetime award.
She was honored at a dinner in New York.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: AH-nur. American honor, honored; British honour, honoured.

entries.meaning: To hold someone's attention so completely that they cannot look away. ---
examples: Her voice mesmerizes a room in about four bars.
The dancer mesmerized the whole theater.
The children sat mesmerized through the puppet show.
entries.contrast: American mesmerize; British usually mesmerise.

entries.meaning: To delight someone completely, as if by magic. ---
examples: Simple melodies enchant small children.
The production enchanted even the hardest critics.
We were enchanted by the costumes.

entries.meaning: To feel great surprise and admiration at something. ---
examples: Visitors still marvel at the ceiling.
She marveled at how quickly he learned the part.
They stood marveling at the size of the canvas.
entries.contrast: You marvel at something. American marveled, marveling with one l; British marvelled, marvelling.

entries.meaning: To play a recording again. ---
examples: They replay the best moments at the end of the show.
He replayed the take a dozen times.
The scene was replayed in slow motion.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed ree-PLAY; the noun replay is REE-play.

entries.meaning: To make a copy of a picture, a sound, or a piece of work. ---
examples: Cheap printing cannot reproduce those colors.
The museum reproduced the fresco at full size.
The drawing has been reproduced on posters and mugs.

entries.meaning: To make something as good as it can possibly be. ---
examples: Dancers spend years perfecting a single turn.
He perfected the trick before showing anyone.
She has perfected that accent.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed pur-FEKT; the adjective perfect is PUR-fikt.

entries.meaning: To make something seem bigger, better, or worse than it really is.
examples: Stage actors exaggerate their gestures a little.
He exaggerated every movement for comic effect.
The features are deliberately exaggerated in the caricature.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (exaggerate a gesture), intransitive (he always exaggerates)
entries.contrast: Double g, and the x sounds like /ɡz/: ig-ZAJ-uh-rayt.
